note: Every fact here is checked against the listed sources. Chapters marked "theory" are fan interpretation, not something the films or their makers confirm.

rabbitHoles.title: The Mind Stone's Trail: Who Held It and What It Did
rabbitHoles.tagline: Why did it seem to affect everyone differently?
rabbitHoles.summary: The Mind Stone passes through a lot of hands: Loki, Hydra, Ultron, Vision and Thanos. Here is every stop it makes on screen, what the films and series actually show it doing, and which part of the popular 'it amplifies you' idea is backed up.
rabbitHoles.payoff: You'll know every on-screen stop the Mind Stone makes, and which parts of the 'it brings out what's already inside you' idea the films really support.

chapters.title: Level 1: Casual Reading
chapters.heading: Where the stone goes
chapters.content: In The Avengers (2012) the Mind Stone sits inside the scepter Loki carries. He uses it to take over the minds of Clint Barton and Erik Selvig, and at the end Natasha Romanoff uses the scepter to close the wormhole over New York. After Loki's defeat the scepter goes to S.H.I.E.L.D. and then to Hydra's Baron Strucker, who is seen with it in the mid-credits scene of Captain America: The Winter Soldier (2014). Age of Ultron (2015) explains that Strucker experimented on people with it, and that Wanda and Pietro Maximoff were the only survivors. In the same film the Avengers take the scepter back, Tony Stark and Bruce Banner find an artificial intelligence inside the gem and use it for the Ultron program, and Ultron takes the stone for a new body that becomes Vision. In Avengers: Infinity War (2018) Thanos tears the stone out of Vision's forehead in Wakanda.

chapters.title: Level 2: Deeper Analysis
chapters.heading: What the stone did to each person
chapters.content: Loki: Wikipedia's Loki article (citing the films) says the scepter controls minds and, without Loki knowing, amplified his hatred for Thor and for the people of Earth. The Avengers itself never spells this out. Wanda: Age of Ultron shows the experiments giving her powers. WandaVision (2021, episode 'Previously On') goes further: the stone amplified magic she already had, and during the experiment she glimpsed herself as the Scarlet Witch. Vision: the stone powers the body Ultron built; Stark and Banner upload J.A.R.V.I.S. into it and Thor's lightning finishes the job. Thanos: for him it is one of six stones he needs for the Infinity Gauntlet.

chapters.title: Level 3: Fan Theory
chapters.heading: Does the stone amplify what's already there?
chapters.content: This part is fan theory, not something the films confirm. A popular reading ties the stone's effects together: it doesn't hand out one fixed power, it boosts what is already inside a person. Two pieces have on-screen support: Loki's hatred being amplified (as the Loki character summary puts it) and Wanda's existing magic being amplified (shown in WandaVision). The idea that the stone shaped Vision's kindness, or worked like a 'mirror' for everyone who touched it, is interpretation only. We could not find a film scene or a statement from Marvel that says so.

corrections: An earlier version of this page said Hydra experimented on the Mind Stone in Iron Man 2. That was wrong: the stone does not appear in Iron Man 2. Hydra's experiments are set up in Captain America: The Winter Soldier's mid-credits scene and explained in Avengers: Age of Ultron.
An earlier version said Ultron stole the stone from Strucker. In Age of Ultron the Avengers take the scepter from Strucker's base, and Ultron takes it from them.

rabbitHoles.title: Tony's Sacrifice: Was It Set Up from the Start?
rabbitHoles.tagline: What the films show, what the filmmakers said, and what is only a fan reading.
rabbitHoles.summary: Tony Stark dies saving everyone at the end of Avengers: Endgame. Looking back, his films keep putting his life on the line. Here's what is on screen, what the writers and directors said about his ending, and why 'it was planned since 2008' isn't backed up.
rabbitHoles.payoff: You'll be able to point to the real moments that build toward Tony's ending, and you'll know the ending itself was shaped from Civil War (2016) onward, not in 2008.

chapters.title: Level 1: Casual Reading
chapters.heading: The moments on screen
chapters.content: Iron Man (2008): shrapnel near his heart leaves Tony relying on an electromagnet, then the arc reactor he and Yinsen build in the cave; once free, he stops Stark Industries making weapons. Iron Man 2 (2010): the palladium core keeping him alive is slowly poisoning him, until he makes a new element from a diagram his father hid. The Avengers (2012): he guides a nuclear missile through the wormhole in what looks like a sacrifice of his own life, and the Hulk catches him as he falls. Iron Man 3 (2013): he has PTSD and panic attacks after New York. Avengers: Endgame (2019): he works out time travel and, in the final battle, uses the Stones to wipe out Thanos and his army, which kills him.

chapters.title: Level 2: Deeper Analysis
chapters.heading: What the filmmakers said
chapters.content: According to Wikipedia's Endgame article, which cites interviews: the writers, Christopher Markus and Stephen McFeely, saw Tony's death as a move to selflessness that closed the chapter he began, and felt he had earned it after getting the retirement he wanted (marriage to Pepper and a daughter). Joe Russo said Tony always knew he would die because he could never stop trying to protect the universe. The same article says the Russo brothers built Tony's final arc starting from Captain America: Civil War (2016) and got Robert Downey Jr.'s approval for it.

chapters.title: Level 3: Fan Theory
chapters.heading: Was it a ten-year plan?
chapters.content: This part is fan reading. Some fans argue Tony's death was mapped out from his very first film. We could not find any statement from Marvel saying that, and the Russo brothers only joined the series with The Winter Soldier (2014). What can be said is that the films keep returning to Tony risking himself, and that the people who wrote and directed Endgame chose to pay that off. Reading earlier films as 'clues' is hindsight, which can be fun, but it isn't evidence of a plan.

corrections: An earlier version of this page quoted Tony saying 'If you die, we die' in Infinity War and listed a value 'answer' for each film. We could not confirm the quote, and the list was our own invention, so both are gone.
An earlier version said the Russo brothers planned ten years of films around this ending. They directed from 2014 and, by their account, shaped Tony's arc from Civil War (2016).

rabbitHoles.title: Loki's Arc: Three Fake Deaths and a Real One
rabbitHoles.tagline: From Thor to Infinity War, what Loki actually does, and how fans read it.
rabbitHoles.summary: Loki 'dies' in Thor, fakes his death in The Dark World, and really dies in Infinity War. Follow what he does in each film, and see where the film record ends and the redemption reading begins.
rabbitHoles.payoff: You'll have Loki's whole film arc straight, including how his last act was trying to save Thor, not Hulk.

chapters.title: Level 1: Casual Reading
chapters.heading: Loki film by film
chapters.content: Thor (2011): Loki learns he is the son of the Frost Giant king Laufey, adopted by Odin. He plans to destroy the Frost Giants' world to prove himself to Odin; when Odin rejects him, he lets himself fall into the abyss. The Avengers (2012): he returns with the scepter, invades New York with the Chitauri, kills Agent Coulson, and is beaten and taken back to Asgard. Thor: The Dark World (2013): after their mother Frigga is killed, he helps Thor, appears to die saving him, and turns out to be alive and disguised as Odin. Thor: Ragnarok (2017): he betrays Thor again on Sakaar, then comes back with a ship to help the Asgardians escape, and the brothers make up. Avengers: Infinity War (2018): he hands Thanos the Tesseract to save Thor's life, pretends to join Thanos, tries to stab him, and is killed.

chapters.title: Level 2: Deeper Analysis
chapters.heading: What the record says about why
chapters.content: Wikipedia's Loki article, citing the films, says he felt neglected by Odin in favour of Thor and grew closer to Frigga, who taught him magic. It also says the scepter he carries in The Avengers amplified his hatred for Thor and Earth without him knowing. On Loki's death, Tom Hiddleston said it was powerful that Loki calls himself an Odinson, and that it closes Loki's journey (quoted in the same article).

chapters.title: Level 3: Fan Theory
chapters.heading: The redemption reading
chapters.content: This part is interpretation. Many fans read Loki's arc as a slow redemption: each 'death' strips away something (his need for Odin's approval, his pride, his habit of running), until in Infinity War he finally puts his brother first. The films support the bookends (rejected by Odin in Thor, dying to protect Thor in Infinity War), but the middle steps are a reading of the story, not something the filmmakers spelled out.

corrections: An earlier version said Loki dies protecting Hulk and that he chooses Thor over escaping with Thanos in Ragnarok. Both were wrong: Thanos is not in Ragnarok, and in Infinity War Loki gives up the Tesseract to save Thor and dies attacking Thanos.

rabbitHoles.title: Did Endgame's Time Heist Break the Multiverse?
rabbitHoles.tagline: What Endgame, Loki and the later films say, and what they don't.
rabbitHoles.summary: The Avengers steal Infinity Stones from 2012, 2013 and 2014. Did that crack open the multiverse? The Loki series gives a surprising answer: the heist itself was 'meant to happen', and the real break came later.
rabbitHoles.payoff: You'll know which timeline problem came from where: Loki's 2012 escape, Sylvie's choice in the Loki finale, and the questions the films still leave open.

chapters.title: Level 1: Casual Reading
chapters.heading: The heist and its rules
chapters.content: In Avengers: Endgame, Bruce Banner explains that changing the past won't change their present; it creates alternate realities instead. In 2012 New York the Ancient One gives Banner the Time Stone only after he promises the Stones will be returned to their proper points in time. The team gets the Mind and Time Stones in 2012, the Reality Stone in 2013 Asgard, and the Power and Soul Stones in 2014. One thing goes wrong in 2012: Loki escapes with the Tesseract (the Space Stone). At the end, Steve Rogers goes back to return the Stones.

chapters.title: Level 2: Deeper Analysis
chapters.heading: What the Loki series adds
chapters.content: Loki season 1 (2021) picks up that escaped 2012 Loki. The Time Variance Authority (TVA) arrests him for creating a new timeline and resets it. When he blames the Avengers, Judge Renslayer says their time travel was meant to happen, unlike his escape. Later, the variant Sylvie sets off TVA reset charges that create many branches. In the finale she kills He Who Remains, which unleashes a multiverse the TVA can't prune. Wikipedia notes that the season sets up Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness (2022) and Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania (2023), where Kang is revealed as a variant of He Who Remains who was exiled by his other variants.

chapters.title: Level 3: Fan Theory and Open Questions
chapters.heading: What's still unanswered
chapters.content: This part is open questions and fan debate. By the Loki series' own rules, the heist did not break anything; Loki's escape did, and the TVA cleaned that up. The wider multiverse opens because of Sylvie in the Loki finale. Some fans still argue the heist must have left other marks: for example, the 2014 Thanos and his army leave their own time and die in 2023. The films never show what happens to that 2014 timeline afterward, so any answer is a guess. We have not found an official statement that settles it.

corrections: An earlier version said the Time Stone was stolen from Doctor Strange in 2018. In Endgame it is given to Banner by the Ancient One in 2012.

An earlier version described 'probability waves' and five destabilised timelines, and said Multiverse of Madness, Quantumania and Loki all trace directly to the heist. None of that is in the films or series, so it has been removed.

rabbitHoles.title: How Vision Came to Life
rabbitHoles.tagline: What makes an AI become a person?
rabbitHoles.summary: Ultron built the body; J.A.R.V.I.S., the Mind Stone and Thor's lightning brought it to life. Here is how Vision was made, what happens to him, and the fan debate about what makes him different from Ultron.
rabbitHoles.payoff: You'll know exactly who made Vision and how, and you'll be able to tell the on-screen facts from the philosophy fans build on top of them.

chapters.title: Level 1: Casual Reading
chapters.heading: How Vision was made
chapters.content: In Avengers: Age of Ultron (2015), Ultron builds himself a new synthetic vibranium body powered by the Mind Stone. The Avengers capture it, and Tony Stark and Bruce Banner upload J.A.R.V.I.S. as its core software. Other Avengers fight to stop them, until Thor uses Mjolnir's lightning to finish the process and Vision comes to life. He sides with the Avengers against Ultron, and wins their trust by lifting Mjolnir and handing it to Thor. He later destroys Ultron and saves Wanda from the falling Sokovian city.

chapters.title: Level 2: Deeper Analysis
chapters.heading: What happens to him
chapters.content: In Avengers: Infinity War (2018), Vision asks Wanda to destroy him and the Mind Stone to keep it from Thanos. In Wakanda she finally does, but Thanos uses the Time Stone to undo it and pulls the stone from Vision's forehead, killing him. In WandaVision (2021), Wanda's grief creates a new Vision inside the Westview 'Hex', while S.W.O.R.D. reactivates the real Vision's body as an all-white Vision. The two talk through the Ship of Theseus puzzle, the Hex Vision restores the other's memories, and the Hex Vision fades when the Hex comes down.

chapters.title: Level 3: Fan Theory
chapters.heading: Why isn't Vision another Ultron?
chapters.content: This part is interpretation. Fans often argue that Ultron is intelligence without conscience while Vision is something closer to a person, and that the Mind Stone (or J.A.R.V.I.S.'s helpful nature) is what tipped him toward protecting life. The films show the result, not the reason: Vision sides with the Avengers because he wants to protect life, and his worthiness to lift Mjolnir is the story's own signal that he can be trusted. Anything beyond that, such as the stone 'granting' consciousness, is a theory the films don't confirm.

corrections: An earlier version said Wanda helped create Vision. She didn't; Stark and Banner uploaded J.A.R.V.I.S. and Thor's lightning activated the body. It also quoted Vision with words we could not confirm, so the quote has been removed.

rabbitHoles.title: Steve Rogers' Ending: Which Timeline Did He Live In?
rabbitHoles.tagline: The directors and the writers gave different answers.
rabbitHoles.summary: At the end of Endgame, Steve returns the Stones, stays in the past with Peggy Carter, and turns up old to hand his shield to Sam Wilson. Did he make a new timeline or live in the main one? Even the people who made the film disagree.
rabbitHoles.payoff: You'll know exactly what the film shows, and that the 'which timeline' question has two official answers, not one.

chapters.title: Level 1: Casual Reading
chapters.heading: What the film shows
chapters.content: After the final battle in Avengers: Endgame (2019), Steve Rogers takes the Infinity Stones and Mjolnir back to their proper times. He doesn't come back the way he left. Instead an elderly Steve is found nearby, and he passes his shield, and the name Captain America, to Sam Wilson. He has stayed in the past with Peggy Carter, married her, and lived a full life. The last scene shows the two of them dancing, the dance he promised her in Captain America: The First Avenger (2011).

chapters.title: Level 2: Deeper Analysis
chapters.heading: Two official answers
chapters.content: Endgame's own rule (explained by Bruce Banner) is that changing the past creates an alternate reality. The directors, Joe and Anthony Russo, have said Steve did create a new timeline when he stayed with Peggy, and later found a way back to the main timeline as an old man. The writers, Christopher Markus and Stephen McFeely, have said Steve found a way to break the rules and lived with Peggy in the main timeline, which would mean two Steves existed at once; they said both were at Peggy's funeral in Captain America: Civil War (2016). Wikipedia's Steve Rogers article records both answers.

chapters.title: Level 3: Fan Theory
chapters.heading: Picking a side
chapters.content: This part is fan debate. The directors' answer fits Endgame's stated time-travel rule but leaves open how Steve got back. The writers' answer explains the old man on the bench neatly but bends the rule the film set up. The film never shows how he returned, so there's no on-screen evidence that settles it. Both readings are made by people who worked on the film, so neither is 'wrong'; it's fair to say the question is genuinely unresolved.

corrections: An earlier version described a 'Bead on a String' model, a 'quantum superposition' and timings such as '70 years in 23 days'. None of those come from the film or its makers, so they have been removed.

rabbitHoles.title: Wanda's Grief and the Darkhold
rabbitHoles.tagline: From Hydra volunteer to the Scarlet Witch of Multiverse of Madness.
rabbitHoles.summary: Wanda loses her parents, her brother and Vision, builds a fake town in WandaVision, and then hunts America Chavez in Multiverse of Madness. Here's what happens, why she does it (it's her sons, not Vision), and the debate over how much of it is the Darkhold.
rabbitHoles.payoff: You'll know what Wanda wants in Multiverse of Madness and why, and you'll see where the official story ends and the fan argument about the Darkhold begins.

chapters.title: Level 1: Casual Reading
chapters.heading: Wanda's story so far
chapters.content: Wanda and her twin Pietro are Sokovian orphans who volunteer for Hydra's experiments with the Mind Stone; they are the only survivors. In Age of Ultron (2015) they first side with Ultron, then join the Avengers, and Pietro dies. In Civil War (2016) she ends up on Steve Rogers' side. In Infinity War (2018) Vision is killed and Wanda is lost in the Blip; she returns for the final battle in Endgame (2019). In WandaVision (2021), after seeing Vision's body being taken apart at S.W.O.R.D., she turns the town of Westview into a sitcom reality with a new Vision and twin sons, Billy and Tommy. In Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness (2022), now the Scarlet Witch and using the Darkhold, she hunts America Chavez to take her power to cross universes and reach a world where she can be with her sons.

chapters.title: Level 2: Deeper Analysis
chapters.heading: Where the Darkhold comes in
chapters.content: At the end of WandaVision, Wanda takes down the Hex, says goodbye to her family and moves to a remote cabin, where she studies the Darkhold to understand her powers and hears her sons calling for help. Wikipedia's Wanda article, summarising Multiverse of Madness, says she is gradually corrupted by the Darkhold. In the film she kills the Earth-838 Illuminati and many sorcerers at Kamar-Taj. When the Earth-838 Billy and Tommy recoil from her in fear, she realises what she has done and brings down Mount Wundagore, destroying every copy of the Darkhold across the multiverse and apparently sacrificing herself.

chapters.title: Level 3: Fan Theory
chapters.heading: Corrupted, or just unleashed?
chapters.content: This part is fan debate. The official summaries say the Darkhold corrupts her. Some fans argue the book only amplified grief and longing that were already there, pointing to WandaVision, where she traps a whole town before she ever reads it. Others felt Multiverse of Madness pushed her too far. Both are opinions about the character; the films don't settle how much of what she does is Wanda and how much is the book.

corrections: An earlier version said Wanda used the Darkhold to find a universe where Vision is alive. In Multiverse of Madness she is trying to reach her sons, Billy and Tommy, not Vision.
An earlier version said she was 'more powerful than Doctor Strange' and that each power came from a specific emotional need. Those were our own claims with no source, so they've been removed.

rabbitHoles.title: Family Bonds in Asgard: Thor, Loki, Odin and Frigga
rabbitHoles.tagline: The adopted-brother story at the heart of the Thor films.
rabbitHoles.summary: Thor is the heir, Loki is the adopted son who finds out late. Follow the family through the Thor films to Infinity War and Endgame, and see where the 'chosen family' reading comes from.
rabbitHoles.payoff: You'll have the Odinson family story straight, film by film, and know which parts are on screen and which are fan reading.

chapters.title: Level 1: Casual Reading
chapters.heading: The family, film by film
chapters.content: Thor (2011): Thor's coronation is interrupted, he is exiled to Earth for disobeying Odin, and Loki learns he is Laufey's son, adopted by Odin after a war. Loki tries to destroy Jotunheim to prove himself to Odin and falls into the abyss when Odin rejects him. Thor: The Dark World (2013): their mother Frigga is killed protecting Jane Foster, and Thor frees Loki so they can avenge her together. Thor: Ragnarok (2017): Odin dies, his firstborn Hela returns, Thor loses his right eye fighting her, and Thor and Loki reconcile aboard the Statesman. Avengers: Infinity War (2018): Loki dies trying to kill Thanos after giving up the Tesseract to save Thor.

chapters.title: Level 2: Deeper Analysis
chapters.heading: Frigga's place in it
chapters.content: Wikipedia's Loki article says Loki felt neglected by Odin in favour of Thor and grew closer to Frigga, who taught him magic. Her death in The Dark World is what makes Thor free Loki in the first place. In Avengers: Endgame (2019), when Thor time-travels to Asgard in 2013, he meets Frigga again and she encourages him.

chapters.title: Level 3: Fan Theory
chapters.heading: The 'chosen family' reading
chapters.content: This part is interpretation. Many fans read the Thor films as a story about chosen family: Loki isn't Odin's son by blood, but by the end he chooses to stand with Thor, and in Infinity War he dies protecting him. It fits what happens on screen, but the films never state it as a theme, and we haven't found a filmmaker quote that does. Take it as one good way to read the story, not the official one.

corrections: An earlier version quoted Loki and Thor with lines we could not confirm ('she was the only one who could've brought me back' and 'We're not so different, you and I') and said Odin adopted Loki as a political move. We couldn't source any of these, so they've been removed.
